draft.title: Comparing purchase options
card: To compare ways to pay, work out the total cost of each: everything you pay in the end, including deposits, fees and interest. The cheapest option is the one with the lowest total.
Cash or debit
you pay the price now from your own money. The total cost is the price, with no interest.
Loan or credit
you pay back the price plus interest and fees over time. Total cost = repayments × number of repayments + any fees.

Example: a $600 phone on a loan costs $55 a month for 12 months. Total = 55 × 12 = $660. That is $60 more than paying $600 cash. Buy now pay later (BNPL) splits the price into instalments. Add up all instalments and any fees in the same way.
draft.remember: Add up everything you pay for each option. The lowest total is the cheapest.

a.q: A $450 bike can be bought on a loan with $40 a month for 12 months. How much more than the cash price does the loan cost?
a.why: Loan total = 40 × 12 = $480. Extra cost = 480 − 450 = $30. The $480 is the total cost, not the extra amount paid.
a.clue: Find the loan total first, then compare it with the cash price.

b.q: Mia buys a $240 jacket. Option A: pay cash. Option B: BNPL with 4 payments of $60 and a $12 late fee she is charged once. Which statement is correct?
opts: Option B costs $12 more than option A
Option B costs $240 in total, the same as A
Option B costs $60 more than option A
Option B costs $12 less than option A
b.why: BNPL instalments are 4 × 60 = $240. Adding the $12 fee gives $252, which is $12 more than the $240 cash price. Splitting the payments does not change the total, but the fee does.
b.clue: Add the instalments and the fee, then compare with the cash price.

b.best: Option B costs $12 more than option A

problems.detail: The card groups credit with loans and says you pay back 'the price plus interest and fees over time'. A credit card paid in full within its interest-free period usually costs no interest, so this misleads students about credit cards.

check.summary: Both questions are correct and well built ($30 and $12 more). The card overstates credit card costs by implying interest is always charged, ignoring interest-free periods.

flags: Card, fact: The card groups credit with loans and says you pay back 'the price plus interest and fees over time'. A credit card paid in full within its interest-free period usually costs no interest, so this misleads students about credit cards.

proposal.title: Comparing purchase options
card: To compare ways to pay, work out the total cost of each: everything you pay in the end, including deposits, fees such as late fees, and interest. The cheapest option has the lowest total.
Cash or debit
you pay the price now from your own money. The total cost is the price, with no interest.
Credit card
you pay later. If you pay the full balance within the interest-free period, there is usually no interest. If not, interest is charged on what is unpaid, and card fees may apply.
Loan or BNPL
you pay in instalments, and loan repayments include interest. Total = instalment × number of instalments + any fees, so $55 a month for 12 months is 55 × 12 = $660.
proposal.remember: Compare the totals you pay in the end, not the size of each instalment.
